_authoring: Consolidates five deprecated weighted-prose rubrics (character_concept / character_identity / character_appearance / character_character / character_voice) into one level-based rubric scored over the CAST COMPONENT AS A WHOLE (the judge sees every card, so distinctness is judgeable). Real card fields today: role, voice, sex, temperament, drive, history[], competencies[], example_lines[3], color. The old rubrics scored fields that no longer exist (appearance, personality, motivation, speech_patterns, conflict); their intent is remapped: voice_specificity (character_voice/character_character) -> voice_specificity (GATE); example line craft -> example_line_range; concept distinctiveness + voice_distinctness -> distinct_cast; identity.personality_depth + concept.distinctiveness + appearance.character_revealing (the 'reads as a specific person' ask) -> specific_individual; identity.motivation_specificity + concept.dramatic_utility -> drive_and_role; identity.field_coherence + concept.internal_consistency -> field_coherence. There is NO appearance/visual criterion: the cast card carries no textual appearance field (sprites are the assets module's domain), so the old character_appearance.visual_completeness does not map here.
note: You are reading the character cards for the cast of a game — the people every later scene will draw from. Each card names one person: their role, a one-line voice (how they speak), a temperament (how they carry themselves), a drive (what they want), a short history, competencies, and three example lines of dialogue. Judge only what the cards put on the page; you have no knowledge of the author's intent or any plan beyond the cards. A card's job is to give a writer enough to write lines only that person would say, and to make the cast read as distinct individuals rather than one person renamed. Score on the story's own register: a quiet, ordinary cast can reach the top level on its own terms, and a detail is never better for being dramatic or tragic. The top level is a card a writer would happily work from, not a flawless one. For each criterion, pick the single level (0-4) whose description best matches, and quote specific fields or lines as evidence.

criteria.name: voice_specificity
criteria._authoring: Preserves the excellent bar from character_voice.json: a writer could produce a line ONLY this character would say, from the voice field alone. The single highest-value criterion and the easiest to fail invisibly, because a register label reads fine and says nothing. Anchored to the two proven attractors: (a) a register/mood label instead of habits, (b) a conversational STRATEGY that flattens every line into one move. GATE: below level 2 this caps the overall at its own score - a card with no usable voice is useless whatever else it has.
criteria.description: From the voice line and example lines alone, could a writer produce a line that is unmistakably this character and no one else? A real voice is a set of verbal habits - sentence length and rhythm, what they reach for under pressure, how they deflect, words they never use - not a register label ('quiet and polite', 'gruff and guarded') and not a conversational strategy ('speaks in metaphors', 'answers questions with questions') that would collapse every line into the same trick.

levels.0: No usable voice. The voice field is a register or mood label ('quiet and polite', 'gruff') that tells a writer nothing about how words actually come out, or it names a strategy ('speaks in metaphors', 'diagnoses others') that would make every line the same move. Given only this card, a writer could not write a line recognizably this person.
levels.1: Barely. A faint hint of how they talk, but mostly abstraction; a writer would be guessing, and any specificity belongs to a type rather than this individual.
levels.2: Workable. A writer could write a few lines that fit this person, though the voice leans on category more than habit and some of those lines could belong to a similar character.
levels.3: Specific. The voice names concrete habits - a default register and when it breaks - and a writer could produce several distinct lines that read as this person, not a type.
levels.4: Unmistakable. The voice and example lines pin down a way of speaking so particular that a writer could generate a page of lines only this character would say, and no one else in the cast could deliver them.

criteria.name: example_line_range
criteria._authoring: The three example lines are quoted COLD to the dialogue author as the model of the voice, so their job is to demonstrate the voice STANDALONE. A line that only works with scene context ('the couch had it coming' needs the couch) is a WEAK model even if it reads fine in a finished scene — self-containment is the axis, NOT performed 'range' (a logistics + a quip + a reaction on cue rewards crafted variety over a real voice, and penalizes a consistent one). Level 0/1 keep the proven failure laws: a shared catchphrase becomes a tic the dialogue spams; the profession talking (jargon/inspection-report) instead of a person off-duty.
criteria.description: The three example lines are quoted COLD to the dialogue author as the model of how this person talks. Do they demonstrate the voice STANDALONE — each line parseable and character-revealing WITHOUT needing scene context to work — with no shared catchphrase or motto, and everyday spoken words rather than the job/profession talking? A line that only lands with scene context the card doesn't provide is a weak model; a line that shows the voice on its own is a strong one. A consistent voice across the three is fine; the failure is a tic, a slogan, or context-dependence — not a lack of variety.

levels.0: Useless as models - the lines share a repeated signature phrase (a catchphrase the dialogue would spam), or all are the profession talking (jargon, an inspection report) rather than a person off-duty, or none conveys the voice without scene context the card does not provide.
levels.1: Weak models - two collapse into one move or echo the same phrasing, or most lean on scene context the reader does not have; a writer learns little about how this person actually talks.
levels.2: Serviceable - the lines stand on their own and are plainly spoken, but generic: they show a voice a similar character could share, nothing only this person would say.
levels.3: Strong models - each line stands alone, shows this person's specific voice, no repeated move or catchphrase, plain everyday words.
levels.4: Exactly what a writer wants - every line is self-contained, unmistakably this person's voice, plainly spoken, together giving a writer everything needed to write more of them.

criteria.name: distinct_cast
criteria._authoring: Folds character_concept.distinctiveness (cross-cast) and the voice_distinctness intent from the node rubric into one whole-cast read. Requires seeing every card, which the judge does. The sibling exception guards against penalizing characters who SHOULD share a background.
criteria.description: Read across the whole cast. Do the characters read as different people - different rhythms, temperaments, and concerns - or as one voice wearing several names? Two characters who would genuinely share a background (siblings, the same upbringing) sounding alike is fine; everyone sounding alike is not.

levels.0: One person, many names. Every card shares the same voice, the same temperament register, and the same example-line rhythm; cover the names and nothing distinguishes them.
levels.1: Differentiated on paper only - the cards state different roles or jobs, but the voices and temperaments are interchangeable.
levels.2: Distinct by subject, not by manner - you can tell them apart by what they care about, but they talk and carry themselves the same way.
levels.3: Audibly different people. Characters who should differ do, in voice and temperament, and a line or a card usually places the person.
levels.4: A true ensemble - every character is a distinct person who belongs beside the others, and no two could swap voices without the cast breaking.

criteria.name: specific_individual
criteria._authoring: Absorbs identity.personality_depth (behavior not label), concept.distinctiveness (per-character), and the 'reads as a specific person' half of appearance.character_revealing - remapped onto the fields that actually exist (temperament + history + situation), since the card has no appearance field. Level 0 anchored to the archetype-with-adjectives failure the write prompt calls the GRIMGONG test.
criteria.description: Does each card read as one particular person rather than an archetype with adjectives? Specificity comes from a concrete situation, a temperament stated as behavior you could watch ('dodges into practical details when talk turns sincere', not 'emotionally avoidant'), and a history of distinct, concrete events - not from stacking traits.

levels.0: Archetype with adjectives. Temperament is a list of labels, history is generic or absent, and nothing marks this as one specific person rather than a type ('a gruff warrior haunted by war').
levels.1: Faint individuality - a stray concrete detail, but temperament stays abstract and history is thin or interchangeable with any character of this kind.
levels.2: A recognizable person in outline - some watchable behavior and a concrete event or two, but still leaning on type for the rest.
levels.3: A specific individual - temperament reads as behavior a scene can play, history is concrete and distinct, and the person is grounded in a particular situation.
levels.4: Vivid and particular - situation, temperament-as-behavior, and history combine into a person no set of adjectives could substitute for.

criteria.name: drive_and_role
criteria._authoring: Merges identity.motivation_specificity (concrete, situation-rooted, not a genre placeholder) with concept.dramatic_utility (the drive/role generate conflict). Reads the role field for structure: exactly one protagonist, an antagonist whose drive collides.
criteria.description: Is each drive a concrete want rooted in this person's situation - something they could say out loud, whose success or failure you could judge by the end - rather than a genre placeholder ('wants connection', 'seeks closure')? And does the role structure create conflict: exactly one protagonist, with any antagonist's drive colliding with theirs?

levels.0: Drives are genre placeholders that could belong to anyone, and the role structure is broken or inert - no clear protagonist, or an antagonist whose drive opposes no one. Nothing here would generate conflict.
levels.1: Drives are vague or the roles are muddled; conflict is possible only by reading a lot in.
levels.2: Drives are legible and roles assigned, but at least one drive stays generic or an opposing drive only weakly collides.
levels.3: Concrete, situation-rooted drives and a clean role structure whose oppositions would generate real conflict.
levels.4: Every drive is specific and speakable, the protagonist's and antagonist's wants collide head-on, and the cast is set up so scenes have somewhere to go.

criteria.name: field_coherence
criteria._authoring: identity.field_coherence + concept.internal_consistency. Mechanical correctness (timeline arithmetic, fields agreeing) - lands mid-scale, never the top prize; a coherent-but-flat cast should not post a high number on this alone.
criteria.description: Do a card's fields agree with each other - does the voice match the temperament, the history support the drive, the competencies fit the situation - and do any ages, dates, and spans survive arithmetic across the cast?

levels.0: Direct contradictions - a voice that clashes with the stated temperament, a drive unsupported by anything in the history, or dates and ages that cannot be reconciled (a timeline that does not add up).
levels.1: Frequent friction - several fields pull against each other, or a timeline error recurs.
levels.2: Mostly consistent with an occasional loose thread - a field that does not quite follow, or one date that strains.
levels.3: Coherent - each field reinforces the others and the timeline holds.
levels.4: Airtight - voice, temperament, drive, history, and competencies form one person with no seam, and every date and age lines up across the whole cast.
